description: Robo plants flowers in a jumble and can't count them. Fox builds them in rows: equal groups, arrays, rows times columns, turning the bed to see 3 × 4 = 4 × 3, finding a missing factor with Bear's carrots and trays, and Fox's split trick for 7 × 4.

youtube.title: Array Garden! Multiplication with Arrays and Equal Groups | Grade 3 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Robo plants flowers all over the garden bed and can't count them. Fox has a better idea: plant in rows! Kids learn that multiplication counts equal groups fast, that an array has equal rows and equal columns (3 rows of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12), and that turning an array doesn't change the product (3 × 4 = 4 × 3). Bear brings missing factor puzzles (4 × ? = 24, ? × 3 = 15), and Fox's split trick breaks 7 × 4 into 5 × 4 + 2 × 4.

For third graders (CCSS 3.OA.A.1, 3.OA.A.3, 3.OA.A.4, 3.OA.B.5, 3.OA.C.7).

Try at home: an egg carton is an array of 2 rows of 6. Put a button or a piece of dry pasta in each cup and say 2 × 6 = 12, then turn the carton and say 6 × 2 = 12. Go on an array hunt: window panes, a muffin tin, floor tiles. Keep buttons and pasta away from babies, and ask a grown-up before using food.

objects.text:
Equal groups and arrays: rows × how many in each row.
Turn it round: the product stays the same.
Missing factor: build it or skip count.
Split a hard fact into two easy ones.

do.text: Array Garden
The garden bed is ready, Robo! Plant the flowers.
Flowers here, flowers there, flowers everywhere!
Hello! I'm Bear, from the plant nursery. How many flowers did you plant?
Easy! One, two, three, four, five...
Six... wait. Did I count this one already?
Oh no. I lost my place. One, two...
A jumble is hard to count. Let's build it in rows and see!
How can we count fast?
First, equal groups. Five pots, and two flowers in each pot.
Count them by twos with me.
Two, four, six, eight, ten!
Five groups of two make ten. In maths, we write five times two equals ten.
The times sign means groups of. Five groups of two.
× means groups of
Now I have three pots. So it's three times something!
Wait. Are these equal groups? Look closely.
Equal groups?
Two, three, two. The groups are not equal.
We only multiply when every group has the same amount.
equal groups: the same in each
Got it. Equal groups first, then times!
Now let's plant an array. An array has equal rows and equal columns.
array: equal rows, equal columns
I'll plant three rows, with four flowers in each row.
How many flowers will that be? Think!
Row by row. Count along!
Four, eight, twelve! Twelve flowers, and I didn't lose my place.
I measure twice. This string shows a row. A row goes across.
This string shows a column. On paper, a column goes up and down.
Three rows and four columns. I know the fact! I'll write it.
Hmm. Three times four is seven? Let's check with the flowers.
You added three and four. But this is three rows of four, not three plus four.
Oops! Three rows of four. Four, eight, twelve.
So three times four equals twelve.
The numbers we multiply are factors. The answer is the product.
Fun fact! The times sign was first printed almost four hundred years ago, in 1631.
× first printed in 1631 by William Oughtred
Here's a puzzle. If we walk round to the side of the bed, will the total change?
Will the total change?
Let's walk round and see!
From this side, I see four rows. Three flowers in each row.
Three, six, nine, twelve. Still twelve!
Four times three equals twelve.
Same garden, same flowers. We just looked from the other side.
So three times four and four times three have the same product.
Turn any array, and the product stays the same. The order of the factors doesn't matter.
turn it: same product
Chant with me! When I say rows, you say times!
Rows!
Times!
Turn it round!
Same amount!
Row by row and plant by plant, equal rows are fast to count!
Turn it round, the same is found!
Tap one finger in the air for every row. Four, eight, twelve!
Farmers plant in straight rows, so they can count, water and pick the crops easily.
My order: six rows, with five flowers in each row.
Tap a finger for each row as we skip count by fives.
Thirty! Six rows of five. Six times five equals thirty.
Next: two long rows, with nine in each row.
Two times nine is eighteen. Now watch me turn the whole bed.
Now it's nine rows of two! Two, four, six... eighteen!
Two times nine equals nine times two. Same flowers, turned around.
I have twenty-four carrots to plant, in four rows. How many go in each row?
Four times what equals twenty-four? The question mark is the missing factor.
? = missing factor
Let's build it and see! One carrot in each row at a time.
Twenty-four! So how many carrots are in each row?
Six columns, so six carrots in each row!
Yes! Four times six equals twenty-four.
Finding a missing factor is how sharing, or division, begins.
Now my seedlings. Fifteen seedlings, three in each tray. How many trays?
Question mark times three equals fifteen. Build it!
Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen. That's five trays!
Five times three equals fifteen. The missing factor is five.
Bear wants seven rows of four. Seven times four is a hard one.
Then I split it into two easy facts. I'll put a little fence after row five.
Above the fence: five rows of four. That's twenty.
Below the fence: two rows of four. That's eight.
Twenty plus eight is twenty-eight!
So seven times four equals twenty-eight. Split a hard fact into two easy ones.
Five times four plus two times four. Built it, checked it!
Garden planners, here are my five orders. Answer each one before Fox does!
Order one: six rows of three pumpkin plants. How many?
Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen. Six times three is eighteen!
Order two: eight times five. What's the product?
Count eight fives: five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, forty!
Eight times five equals forty.
Order three: what times six equals thirty-six?
Six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, thirty, thirty-six. Six sixes! The missing factor is six.
Order four: do two rows of nine and nine rows of two have the same total?
Yes! Turn the bed round. Both are eighteen.
Order five: use the split trick for six times four.
Five fours are twenty, and one more four makes twenty-four.
Six times four equals twenty-four. All five orders, done!
Quiz time! Question one: four rows of five sunflowers. How many?
Four times five is twenty.
Question two: three times seven is twenty-one. So what is seven times three?
Twenty-one! Turn the array, same product.
Question three: five times what equals thirty-five?
Seven! Five times seven is thirty-five.
Question four: which shows multiplication? Pots with four, four and four, or four, two and five?
Four, four and four. Those are equal groups.
Question five: split six times seven into five sevens and one seven.
Thirty-five plus seven is forty-two!
Today we learned: arrays have equal rows. Rows times how many in each row.
Turn an array round, and the product stays the same.
Build it or skip count to find a missing factor, and split hard facts.
Best garden in town! Here's your ribbon.
Built it, checked it, twice!
Go find an array at home: an egg carton, a muffin tin, or windows. Bye!
